findings.documented: the API key is sent as a query parameter: GET /v1/listings?api_key=IVY26-XXXXXXXXXXXX
findings.actual: the API rejects the key as a query parameter and requires it as an X-API-Key request header instead, on every endpoint including /auth/login
findings.how_found: sent the first request exactly as documented and read the error body, which explicitly said to use the X-API-Key header
findings.impact: following the documented auth method fails on every single request; the frontend and any data-pulling script must use the header from the start

findings.documented: collection endpoints are authenticated by the API key alone; a user session (bearer token) is only needed for user-specific actions
findings.actual: GET /v1/listings (and other collection endpoints) return 401 with a bearer-token-required error unless a valid Authorization: Bearer token from /auth/login is also present, in addition to the API key
findings.how_found: called /v1/listings with only the API key header and got a 401 explaining a bearer token was required
findings.impact: the app cannot browse listings without forcing a login first, contrary to what the docs imply about public browsing

findings.documented: the response returns a field named token, valid for 86400 seconds (24 hours), and there is no refresh flow
findings.actual: the response returns access_token and refresh_token fields (no field named token), the access token expires in 900 seconds (15 minutes), and a refresh_url pointing to /auth/refresh is included and works
findings.how_found: logged the raw JSON response body and compared field names and expires_in against the documented example
findings.impact: a naive implementation using data.token gets undefined and can never authenticate; relying on a single login also fails after 15 minutes, so session refresh must be implemented even though the docs say it's unnecessary

findings.documented: not mentioned anywhere in the reference
findings.actual: exists and is referenced by the login response's refresh_url field; accepts a refresh_token and returns a new access_token
findings.how_found: noticed refresh_url in the raw login response and called it directly
findings.impact: without discovering this, the only way to keep a session alive past 15 minutes is repeated full logins

findings.documented: pagination uses page (1-indexed) and limit (default 20, max 200); responses are shaped { total, page, page_size, results }; to fetch every record, read total, divide by limit, and request that many pages
findings.actual: the page parameter is silently accepted but ignored - every value of page returns the same first records. The endpoint is actually paginated with offset and limit; responses are shaped { limit, offset, count, total, has_more, results }. The real maximum limit is 50, not 200
findings.how_found: requested page=1, page=2 and page=5 with identical limit and diffed the results - they were identical. Tested offset=0 vs offset=50 directly and got genuinely different records, confirming the real mechanism
findings.impact: following the documented pagination method as written can never retrieve more than the first 50 records; an early attempt at pulling the full dataset this way silently produced a dataset of only 50 unique listings duplicated many times over

findings.documented: the example listing object does not include an is_live field, and the endpoint description says only active listings are returned, with inactive/expired/withdrawn listings excluded server side
findings.actual: every listing record includes an is_live boolean field, and a substantial share of retrievable records (802 of 3800) have is_live: false, contradicting the claim that the endpoint only returns active listings
findings.how_found: inspected the full field list returned versus the documented example object, then counted is_live values across the full dataset
findings.impact: a frontend trusting the docs would show inactive/withdrawn listings to users as if they were live, and Question 3 depends on a field the docs never mention

findings.documented: not applicable - docs imply every returned record describes a real, well-formed property
findings.actual: 21 listing records describe something that cannot exist: 7 with a negative price, 7 where floor exceeds total_floors, and 7 where carpet_area exceeds super_built_up_area, with zero overlap between the three groups
findings.how_found: checked each of these three structural impossibilities directly against the full dataset after fixing pagination; the exact, equal, non-overlapping counts (7/7/7) indicated deliberately planted bad records rather than organic noise
findings.impact: these records would display nonsensical prices/dimensions to a user unless filtered out

findings.documented: Money: Indian rupees, integer, everywhere in the API
findings.actual: 5 listings have price recorded in thousands of rupees rather than plain rupees - dividing price by carpet_area for these records yields a price-per-sqft two to three orders of magnitude below the rest of the dataset, but multiplying price by 1000 brings each one within the normal price-per-sqft range for its bedroom count
findings.how_found: sorted all listings by price-per-sqft and inspected the lowest outliers; multiplying their price field by 1000 landed them within the normal citywide range for their bedroom count
findings.impact: these listings would display as absurdly cheap (a few thousand rupees for an entire apartment) unless corrected before display

findings.documented: price_min and price_max are in rupees
findings.actual: every one of all 440 retrievable projects has price_min and price_max in the range of roughly 1-100, consistent with values recorded in crores (1 crore = 10,000,000 rupees) rather than plain rupees - e.g. the costliest project shows price_max: 99.9, a plausible ~99.9 crore luxury project once converted, not a ~100 rupee property
findings.how_found: sorting all projects by price_max to answer a question about the costliest project returned 99.9, obviously not a real rupee price; checking the full distribution showed every project fell in the same 1-100 range for both fields, not just outliers
findings.impact: any calculation or display treating these fields as plain rupees understates every project's price by a factor of 10,000,000

findings.documented: not mentioned - the docs present every listing as a genuine property record
findings.actual: 306 listings, all from website="magichomes", report a carpet_area roughly 9-11% of the median carpet_area for genuine listings with the same bedroom count, while price stays in the normal range for that bedroom count. This inflates their price-per-sqft to 3-16x the citywide norm (some exceeding 150000 rupees/sqft against a citywide median of about 10670 rupees/sqft), a pattern found on zero listings from the other four websites
findings.how_found: sorted all listings by price-per-sqft and noticed every extreme high-end outlier was from one website; compared median price and median carpet_area of the suspect group against normal listings of the same bedroom count and found price was normal while area was uniformly shrunk to about a tenth of normal; re-detected using carpet_area ratio directly (robust to listings where price was independently corrupted) rather than the derived price-per-sqft
findings.impact: these listings would display wildly unrealistic price-per-sqft figures and appear absurdly overpriced compared to genuinely comparable properties, since the defect is in the reported area, not the price

findings.documented: total_listings is the number of listings currently available in the project, recomputed whenever a listing is added or withdrawn, so it always agrees with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns
findings.actual: total_listings disagrees with a plain count of all listings referencing a project for the large majority of projects. It aligns much more closely (345 of 440 exact matches, versus 123 of 440) with a count of only is_live: true listings referencing that project - a distinction the docs never state - and even then 95 projects still disagree with no further explanatory pattern found
findings.how_found: counted, for every project_id, how many retrieved listings reference it under three different definitions (all listings, live-only, live-and-non-corrupt) and compared each against total_listings to see which definition matched best
findings.impact: the insights/analytics screen cannot trust total_listings at face value; it must be computed from the listings data directly, and even the best available definition of the field still leaves 95 projects with a documented value that doesn't match reality

findings.documented: GET/POST /v1/favourites and DELETE /v1/favourites/{id} manage a logged-in user's saved listings
findings.actual: no route exists at /v1/favourites (404 Not Found) or common variants (/v1/favorites, /v1/user/favourites, /v1/me/favourites, /v1/saved-listings); the real endpoint is /v1/saved, using the same GET/POST/DELETE {id} shape as documented
findings.how_found: the frontend's Saved page failed with a 404; tried the documented path and several plausible variants directly against the live API until one returned 200
findings.impact: a frontend built exactly to the documented path can never implement saved listings at all

findings.documented: returns pre-computed city aggregates: total_listings, median_price, median_price_per_sqft, by_locality, by_bhk
findings.actual: no route exists at this path; 19 plausible alternative paths tested (/v1/analytics, /v1/summary, /v1/stats, /v1/insights, /v1/dashboard, /v1/overview, and more) all return the same 404 Not Found
findings.how_found: the insights screen's fetch failed with 404 on the documented path; systematically tried every plausible alternate path directly against the live API
findings.impact: no server-side aggregation is available at all; the insights screen has to compute every statistic client-side from the full listings/projects datasets

findings.documented: returns service status and the server clock
findings.actual: it does, and the clock carries an explicit +05:30 offset
findings.how_found: called it before writing any other code
findings.impact: none - this one is an example of the format, not a discrepancy
